chunks: The Sheikh, may God have mercy on him, informed me, from Abu Ja'far Muhammad b. Ali, from his father, from Muhammad b. Yahya, from Muhammad b. Ahmad b. Yahya, from Musa b. Ja'far, from Ali b. Sa'id, from Ubaydallah b. al-Dahqan, from Abu Khalid,

he said: 'Wash all the dead — the drowned one, the one devoured by a wild beast, and everything else — except what was killed between the two battle lines. If there was still a breath of life in him, he shall be given ghusl; otherwise, no.'

key_terms.الصَّفَّيْنِ: the two battle lines; the battlefield context that defines the martyrdom exception to ghusl
key_terms.الْغَرِيقَ: the drowned one; one who died by drowning, explicitly included in the ghusl obligation
key_terms.الْمَوْتَى: the dead; all deceased persons for whom ritual washing is obligatory
key_terms.رَمَقٌ: a breath of life; the last remaining flicker of life in a dying person, used as a legal criterion

ai.seo_question: Does a martyr killed between two battle lines receive ghusl in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith establishes a key fiqh ruling: ghusl al-mayyit (ritual washing of the dead) is obligatory for all deceased persons, including those who drowned or were mauled by wild animals. The sole exception is the martyr killed between two battle lines (bayna al-saffayn), and even this exception is conditional — if any breath of life (ramaq) remained in him when removed from the field, ghusl must still be performed.
word_analysis: may He have mercy on him
